segments.english: He said to him, "Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."
segments.literal: and-said to-him take for-me heifer tripled and-she-goat tripled and-ram tripled and-turtledove and-young-bird

tokens.note: wayyiqtol
imperative with paragogic he, which adds urgency
Pual participle of the denominative verb 'to do in threes'; see note
masculine form, agreeing with the ram

phrases.literal: heifer tripled; read as three years old (Ibn Ezra); Rashi: three heifers
and-young-bird; the young of the dove (Rashi, Ibn Ezra)

grammar: קְחָה is the imperative with the paragogic ה, a mark of urgency or courtesy.
מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת / מְשֻׁלָּשׁ is a Pual participle (feminine, then masculine) of שָׁלַשׁ; it agrees in gender with each animal.
The accents group the three large animals, each with its participle, and the etnaḥta falls on מְשֻׁלָּשׁ; the two birds follow as a separate pair.
The list is in a fixed order of three animals and two birds; the birds take no participle.
segments.note: מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת can mean 'three-year-old' (BDB: Pu three years old; Ibn Ezra's choice) or 'threefold', i.e. three of each (Rashi, Onkelos). I read 'three-year-old' and record the other in the commentary. הַגּוֹזָל is any young bird; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the young of the dove, which fits the pairing with the turtledove.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'three calves', an allusion to three bullocks (the Day of Atonement bullock, the community's bullock for an inadvertent error, and the heifer whose neck is broken). The English reads the Pual participle as an age instead.

Rashi: the three goats allude to the goat offered inside, the goats of the festival additional offerings, and an individual's sin-offering goat. This follows his 'threefold' reading and is not adopted.
Rashi: the three rams allude to the certain guilt offering, the suspended guilt offering, and an individual's sin-offering lamb; this too follows 'threefold'.
Rashi, citing Bereshit Rabbah: the turtledove and the young of a dove. The English 'young pigeon' follows.
Ibn Ezra: some say three goats, but 'it is right in my eyes' that the goat was three years old. The English reads three-year-old.
Ibn Ezra: אַיִל is the large lamb (כבש). The English 'ram' keeps the animal as the grown male sheep.
Ibn Ezra: גוֹזָל is the young dove, since only these are named among beasts and birds for burnt offerings and every sacrifice. The English follows.

apparatus: Onkelos reads three of each ('three heifers, three goats, three rams'), against Ibn Ezra's three-year-old.
Radak notes that גּוֹזָל can name the young of any bird, citing Deut 32:11, but takes it here as the young dove.

segments.english: He took all these for him, cut them in the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not cut in two.
segments.literal: and-took for-him OBJ all-of these and-cut them in-the-midst and-gave man piece-his to-meet fellow-his and-OBJ the-bird not cut

tokens.note: wayyiqtol
the antecedent of 'him' is God, for whom the animals are taken (Rashi); the pronoun is left unmarked in the English
Piel wayyiqtol; the verb is used of dividing animals for a covenant
בַּ = ב + the article
wayyiqtol of נתן in the sense of setting in place
אִישׁ is used distributively, 'each one'
construct noun with suffix, 'his piece'
לִקְרַאת is the infinitive construct of קרא 'to meet'; here 'opposite'
'his companion'
collective singular
qatal; the word order puts the object first, in contrast

phrases.english: He took all these for him

phrases.literal: and-cut OBJ-them in-the-midst; Rashi: he divided each into two
to-meet fellow-his; each piece facing its fellow

phrases.english: but the birds he did not cut in two
phrases.literal: and-OBJ the-bird not cut; collective singular 'bird', understood as the two birds (Ibn Ezra)

grammar: The object is fronted in וְאֶת־הַצִּפֹּר לֹא בָתָר, which sets the birds against the animals: the animals were cut, the birds were not.
אִישׁ בִּתְרוֹ לִקְרַאת רֵעֵהוּ is a distributive phrase, 'each one its piece opposite its fellow', as in Exod 26:3 (Ibn Ezra).
The verb בָּתַר ('to cut in two') recurs here three times and gives the passage its name, בֵּין הַבְּתָרִים.
The etnaḥta at רֵעֵהוּ closes the first half: the cutting and setting out of the animals.
segments.note: The text does not say who commanded the cutting; the commentators take it as part of the covenant rite. צִפֹּר is a collective singular; Ibn Ezra reads it as the turtledove and the young pigeon of v. 9, which I follow. The pointing הַצִּפֹּר is that of the base text; WLC reads הַצִפֹּר without the dagesh. בֶּתֶר at 15:10.11 is listed in the lexicon only with the sense 'cleft mountains', which does not fit here; I give no sense number and read 'piece, half', as the lexicon's gloss says.

commentary.summary: Rashi: he divided each into two parts, for he was making a covenant, and covenant-makers divide animals and pass between the pieces (Jer 34:18). The smoking oven and flaming torch that pass between the pieces are the messenger of the Presence.
Rashi: the nations are likened to bulls, rams and goats and Israel to doves, so the animals were cut as a sign that the nations will be consumed; a homiletic reading, not about the wording.
Rashi: the birds were not cut as a sign that Israel will endure for ever; the second half of the same homily.
Ibn Ezra: וַיְבַתֵּר means 'he cut them and separated them', as in 'the mountains of Bether' (Song 2:17) and 'between its parts' (Jer 34:18).

Ibn Ezra: אִישׁ is like בַּעַל, as in 'man of war' and 'worthless man'; it is a distributive form like 'one to her sister' (Exod 26:3). He placed each piece of each animal opposite its fellow, since beast and bird are two kinds.
Ibn Ezra: הַצִּפֹּר is the turtledove and the young pigeon, because צִפּוֹר is a general term.

apparatus: 15:10.15 vowels: WLC reads הַצִפֹּ֖ר (no dagesh in the צ); base text הַצִּפֹּ֖ר. Meaning unchanged.

Ramban records that the birds were not cut because of the rule of Lev 1:17 (the bird burnt offering is not divided) and notes Bereshit Rabbah on the difference between burnt-offering and sin-offering birds; not adopted as the plain sense.

segments.english: The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them off.
segments.literal: and-came-down the-bird-of-prey upon the-carcasses and-caused-to-blow them Abram

tokens.note: wayyiqtol
collective singular, 'birds of prey'
the definite article marks 'the' carcasses just prepared
Hifil wayyiqtol of נשב, 'to cause to blow'; the nun is assimilated, so the shin is doubled

phrases.english: The birds of prey came down on the carcasses

phrases.literal: and-caused-to-blow them Abram; Rashi: 'blowing away', making them fly off

grammar: וַיַּשֵּׁב is a Hifil wayyiqtol of נשב ('to blow'), with the doubled shin standing for the assimilated nun; it means 'he blew them off'.
הָעַיִט is a collective singular with a singular verb: 'the birds of prey'.
The etnaḥta on הַפְּגָרִים divides the verse; the second half gives Abram's response.
The subject Abram stands last, after the object, a mark of emphasis on what he did.
segments.note: הַפְּגָרִים are the bodies of the animals that Abram had just cut up (Rashi: 'the pieces'; Ibn Ezra: 'the bodies'), so I write 'carcasses'. Radak argues that פְּגָרִים are whole bodies, i.e. the two birds; not adopted. For וַיַּשֵּׁב, Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take 'to blow away, make fly off'; Ibn Ezra also offers 'he made the carcasses return to drive off the bird', recorded in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the עַיִט is a bird that swoops and gasps after carrion, from עָט as in 'and you swooped upon the spoil' (1 Sam 15). The English 'birds of prey' follows.
Rashi: 'on the carcasses' means on the pieces. He argues against the Targums that render it as pieces (פלגיא), since פגרים is related to פגול.
Rashi: וַיַּשֵּׁב is 'blowing and making fly', as in 'he makes his wind blow' (Ps 147). The English 'drove off' follows; the allusion to David and the Messiah is not applicable to the plain sense.
Ibn Ezra: עַיִט is a bird, as in 'the speckled bird of prey is my inheritance' (Jer 12:9).
Ibn Ezra: פְּגָרִים are the bodies.

Ibn Ezra: the shin has a dagesh in place of the absorbed nun, like יְגָרֵשׁ, 'he drove them away from the carcasses', as in 'he makes his wind blow' (Ps 147:18); or alternatively 'he returned the carcasses to drive off the bird'.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra's alternative: וַיַּשֵּׁב from שׁוּב, 'he put the carcasses back' to scare off the bird; the English keeps the נשב reading, the one the lexicon lists.
Onkelos renders 'and Abram scared them away' (וְאַפְרַח), in line with 'to blow away'.

segments.english: As the sun was about to go down, a deep sleep fell on Abram, and suddenly dread, a great darkness, was falling on him.
segments.literal: and-was the-sun to-go-in and-deep-sleep fell upon Abram and-behold dread darkness great falling upon-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; with a time clause it marks the setting, 'it happened that'
לָבוֹא, 'to go in'; the sun 'goes in' when it sets
qatal, feminine to agree with תַּרְדֵּמָה
וְהִנֵּה draws the reader into what Abram sees or feels
active participle, feminine; it describes a state that continues

phrases.english: As the sun was about to go down
a deep sleep fell on Abram
phrases.literal: and-deep-sleep fell upon Abram; the same word as in 2:21

phrases.english: and suddenly dread, a great darkness, was falling on him
phrases.literal: and-behold dread darkness great falling upon-him; the nouns stand side by side

grammar: וַיְהִי with a time clause (הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לָבוֹא) is a standard way to open a new scene: 'the sun was about to set'.
The word order moves from qatal (נָפְלָה) to a participle (נֹפֶלֶת): the deep sleep falls, then the dread continues to fall.
אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה: three words in a row, 'terror, darkness, great'; the adjective is feminine and may modify חֲשֵׁכָה alone or both nouns.
הִנֵּה brings the reader into Abram's experience.
segments.note: The three nouns אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה can be read as a list ('a dread, a darkness, great') or as 'a dread of great darkness' or 'a great, dark dread'. The English keeps the apposition: 'dread, a great darkness'. The lexicon lists no sense for גָּדוֹל that matches 'great' (it lists 'loud', 'do great things', 'greatness'), so I give none at 15:12.11.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the dread and darkness are an allusion to the troubles and darkness of the exiles; a reading of the vision, not of the wording.
Ibn Ezra: 'the sun was about to set' is a sign that Abram took all these on one day, since he woke from the prophetic vision. The English reads the sunset as the same day's setting.

segments.english: He said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs, and they will serve them, and they will oppress them, for four hundred years.
segments.literal: and-said to-Abram knowing you-will-know that sojourner will-be your-seed in-land not to-them and-they-will-serve-them and-they-will-oppress OBJ-them four hundreds year

tokens.note: wayyiqtol
infinitive absolute, to intensify the finite verb
yiqtol; with the infinitive absolute, 'you will surely know'
singular גֵּר with the collective subject זַרְעֲךָ, hence 'sojourners'
yiqtol
זֶרַע is a collective singular
לָהֶם, 'to them'; the land does not belong to them
a perfect with wāw-consecutive, continuing the future
a perfect with wāw-consecutive; the subject is the people of the land

phrases.literal: knowing you-will-know; the infinitive absolute strengthens the verb

phrases.english: that your offspring will be sojourners
phrases.literal: that sojourner will-be your-seed; collective singular
in-land not to-them; the land is not theirs (Rashi)

phrases.english: and they will serve them, and they will oppress them

grammar: יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע is the infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root: 'you shall surely know'.
The accents join the clause 'your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not theirs' and then close it at the zaqef; the next verbs are a new clause, whose subject shifts without being named.
The perfects with wāw (וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ) continue the future: 'and they will serve, and will afflict'.
אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the number of years in apposition: the period comes at the end.
segments.note: In וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם the subject and object are not named; 'they will serve them … and they will oppress them' keeps that ambiguity, where 'they' is the people of the land. Whether 'four hundred years' counts the whole period or only the oppression is also open: Rashi counts four hundred years from the birth of Isaac, and Ibn Ezra counts from the day of the vision; the English keeps the number without fixing its starting point. Rashi's point that 'a land not theirs' is not only Egypt is followed.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the four hundred years run from the birth of Isaac until Israel left Egypt (Isaac sixty at Jacob's birth, Jacob 130 at the descent, 210 years in Egypt), and he shows that the time in Egypt alone was less. The English does not fix the starting point.
Rashi: it does not say 'in the land of Egypt' but 'a land not theirs': from Isaac's birth Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all sojourned in the land. The English 'a land not theirs' follows.
Ibn Ezra: the גֵּר is like the grain cut from the branch, as the אֶזְרָח is the man with a family, like the branch attached to the root. The English takes the ordinary sense 'sojourner'.
Ibn Ezra: the four hundred years run 'to the end of this term from today'. The English leaves the starting point open.

segments.english: And also the nation that they will serve, I will judge; and afterward they will come out with great wealth.
segments.literal: and-also OBJ the-nation that they-will-serve judging I and-after thus they-will-go-out with-property great

tokens.note: גַּם adds a further point: not only is the descendants' lot told, but the nation will be judged
yiqtol, 3rd plural
participle; the Hebrew puts it before 'I' for emphasis
yiqtol, 3rd plural

phrases.english: And also the nation that they will serve
phrases.literal: and-also OBJ the-nation that they-will-serve; the object stands first, for emphasis
judging I; participle, 'I am judging', with the future sense

phrases.english: they will come out with great wealth

grammar: The object וְגַם אֶת־הַגּוֹי is placed first, before the subject אָנֹכִי; this puts the weight on the nation that will be judged.
דָּן is a participle ('judging'), which here gives a near-future sense: 'I am about to judge'.
אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ is a relative clause without a resumptive pronoun: 'the nation that they will serve'.
בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל, 'with great property', returns to the Exodus; the verb יֵצְאוּ matches the 'exodus' formula.
segments.note: The word order of the Hebrew puts the object first, and the English follows it. Rashi takes גַּם to add the four kingdoms to Egypt; this is recorded rather than adopted. Ibn Ezra's gloss for אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ ('so that they have servants') fits the plain sense of the nation as master.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'also' adds the four kingdoms, since they too will be destroyed for enslaving Israel. The English keeps 'also' without naming the kingdoms.
Rashi: the judgment is 'by ten plagues'. A more specific reading than the Hebrew states; recorded.
Rashi: בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל is 'with great wealth', as it says 'and they stripped Egypt' (Exod 12). The English follows.
Ibn Ezra: אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ means that the nation will have servants, i.e. the nation that they will serve. The English follows.

segments.english: As for you, you will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried at a good old age.
segments.literal: and-you you-will-come to your-fathers in-peace you-will-be-buried in-old-age good

tokens.note: וְאַתָּה with a contrastive sense: 'but you', 'as for you'
yiqtol, 2nd singular
plural construct with suffix, 'your fathers'
Nifal yiqtol, passive
שֵׂיבָה is the grey hair of age

phrases.literal: and-you; the pronoun sets Abram against his offspring

phrases.english: you will go to your fathers in peace
phrases.literal: you-will-come to your-fathers in-peace; a euphemism for death (Ibn Ezra)

phrases.english: you will be buried at a good old age

grammar: וְאַתָּה with the separate pronoun contrasts Abram with his descendants, who suffer in the previous verses.
תָּבוֹא אֶל־אֲבֹתֶיךָ is a euphemism for death, 'come to your fathers' (Ibn Ezra).
תִּקָּבֵר is a Nifal, 'you will be buried', passive of קבר.
בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה means 'in a good old age'; the adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender.
segments.note: תָּבוֹא is rendered 'you will go': Hebrew בוא is 'come' or 'go in', and English 'go to your fathers' is the usual idiom for death. The lexicon sense used is Qal 4, 'go'. Rashi's comments on the repentance of Terah and Ishmael use the verse for homily and do not bear on the plain sense.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'you will come' means that Abram will not see all this (the exile). It adds a reason and is not a statement about the Hebrew's wording.
Rashi: Terah served idols, so 'to your fathers' teaches that Terah repented; a homily.
Rashi: 'a good old age' is a promise that Ishmael will repent and Esau will not go to bad ways in Abraham's days; a homily on the timing of Abraham's death.
Ibn Ezra: 'come to your fathers' is a figure for death, 'the way of all the earth'. The English 'go to your fathers' follows.
Ibn Ezra: בְּשָׁלוֹם means 'in honour, and not as your offspring'. The English keeps 'in peace', which can bear that sense.

segments.english: And in the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not complete until now.
segments.literal: and-generation fourth they-will-return hither for not complete iniquity-of the-Amorite until hither

tokens.note: 'generation' (BDB 2) is singular, with a plural verb in agreement with its collective sense
yiqtol, 3rd plural; the subject is the offspring, 'the generation'
הֵנָּה is 'hither', toward this land
adjective, 'whole, full'
construct
collective singular, 'the Amorite'
'to this point'; the same word as 15:16.4, in a different sense (time)

phrases.english: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not complete

grammar: וְדוֹר רְבִיעִי is a singular noun with a plural verb (יָשׁוּבוּ): the 'generation' stands for its members.
הֵנָּה ('here') appears twice in the verse, once of place (in the land) and once of time (up to now: עַד־הֵנָּה).
The reason clause כִּי לֹא־שָׁלֵם עֲוֺן הָאֱמֹרִי states why the promise is delayed: the Amorites' guilt is not yet full.
The etnaḥta on הֵנָּה ends the first half, the return; the second half gives the reason.
segments.note: I follow Rashi in taking דּוֹר as 'generation' (BDB sense 2), so four generations: Jacob and his sons into Egypt, then the fourth generation returns. Ibn Ezra reads דּוֹר as 'a dwelling' of the lifetime of a person and also counts to the fourth after the sojourn; I record this. The Amorites are a collective singular; the word 'iniquity' is kept, and not softened to 'guilt'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: after they go down to Egypt there will be three generations there and in the fourth they return to this land (Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb son of Hezron came into the land). The English 'fourth generation' follows.

Rashi: Israel's return is delayed because God does not exact payment from a nation until its measure is full, as in 'in measure, when you send her away, you contend with her' (Isa 27). The English follows.

Ibn Ezra: most commentators err about 'generation'; דּוֹר means a dwelling (as in 'to dwell in the tents of wickedness', Ps 84:11), measured by the span of a person's life, long or short. The fourth after they are strangers in Egypt: Kohath, Amram, Moses and Aaron, and their sons returned to Canaan.

Ibn Ezra: 'iniquity' is as in 'my iniquity is greater than I can bear' (Gen 4:13). The Amorite is named because of his strength; Moses killed the great kings, who were Amorite kings, and the five kings of the Amorites gathered against Joshua.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra rejects deriving הָאֱמֹרִי from אמר ('to say'); the Amorites are named for their strength, as in Amos 2:9.
